tier_reason: The README gives only a first-party ratio ('about 4-6 times faster than GNU coreutils' wc') with no timings, file, hardware, GNU wc version, locale or benchmark script; the author's write-ups (0xd34df00d.me post, Habr article) do not resolve from here, so no methodology could be checked.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: stack.yaml resolver lts-15.2 (GHC 8.8 series, bytestring 0.10.10.0) with package.yaml ghc-options -fllvm -O2 -Wall and executable RTS option -with-rtsopts=-A2m; LLVM version not stated. GNU wc version, build flags and the locale it ran in are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are a single ratio sentence in the README with no hardware, file size, GNU wc version, locale or timing method; the author's Habr article ('Побеждая C двадцатью строками Haskell: пишем свой wc', Feb 2020) and blog post could not be opened (hosts do not resolve here). hwc does less work than GNU wc: src/Data/WordCount.hs splits words on ASCII whitespace only (bytes 9-13 and 32), counts characters as non-continuation bytes without UTF-8 validation, and counts every byte >= 32 as one column for max line length (no display-width handling, so -L is wrong for multibyte text), whereas GNU wc in a UTF-8 locale decodes multibyte characters. The line count is Data.ByteString.count, which in bytestring 0.10.10.0 calls the C helper c_count (fps_count), so the -l path is C code; input is mmapped via bytestring-mmap. Habr search snippets (snippet only) describe a third-party response that measured, on a 1.8 GB file, system wc 19.416 s, a simple Haskell version 2.811 s, a simple C version 3.067 s and an optimized hand-written single-threaded C version 0.637 s, so the gap is to GNU wc's general implementation, not to C; a Habr commenter also notes the simplified spec (Unicode ignored). Measured against a 2020 coreutils; later coreutils releases (which reworked wc's line counting) were not compared. Abandoned since March 2020.
corrections.why_faster: Not a language effect: hwc computes only the requested statistics with branchless byte folds over an mmapped file, treats words and line width as ASCII (no multibyte decoding or wcwidth), and its line count is bytestring's C helper fps_count; GNU wc runs a general locale-aware loop. A hand-written single-threaded C version beat the Haskell versions in a third-party Habr reply (snippet only).

notes: Confirm at C; README ratio matches the record. Shortcomings: ratio-only claim with no methodology, reduced work versus GNU wc (ASCII-only words and line width, no UTF-8 validation), the -l path is bytestring's C code, and a third-party hand-written C wc was faster (snippet only); same_algorithm set to false. Not a language-level win.

tier_reason: First-party criterion benchmark with public code (resharp-engine/examples/popular-crates.rs, driven by scripts/bench-popular-table.mts), release-profile flags in Cargo.toml and the CPU (Ryzen 7 5800X) stated, but the rustc version is unpinned and PCRE2's version, source (bundled or system) and C build flags are not stated, so it falls short of A. The POPL 2025 paper covers the .NET implementation (already catalogued), not this Rust rewrite.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README scan table (find_all over a 1 MiB haystack), resharp vs PCRE2 (JIT): faster on 12 of 19 patterns, a tie on 1 ("([^"]+)" 5.44 vs 5.43 GiB/s), slower on 6 (counted from the table). Examples: \d+ 1.76 GiB/s vs 358.25 MiB/s (5.03x), .* 2.27 GiB/s vs 768.24 MiB/s (3.03x), \d+\.\d+\.\d+ 4.86 GiB/s vs 395.43 MiB/s (12.59x), \n{3,} 19.68 vs 6.61 GiB/s (2.98x). PCRE2 faster: <[^>]+> 2.61 vs 2.09 GiB/s, \$\{([^}]+)\} 10.66 vs 5.63 GiB/s, <[^>]*> 3.01 vs 2.82 GiB/s, `([^`]+)` 14.17 vs 12.99 GiB/s, markdown link 5.65 vs 4.99 GiB/s, and (?is)<script[^>]*>.*?</script> 7.08 GiB/s vs 807.97 MiB/s (8.97x in PCRE2's favour). Validate latency vs PCRE2: resharp faster on 3 of 6 (^$ 2.76 vs 18.56 ns, ISO date 22.88 vs 27.97 ns, ^\d+$ 24.04 vs 30.05 ns), slower on 3 (email 43.45 vs 36.22 ns, identifier 35.05 vs 32.37 ns, slug 35.67 vs 29.66 ns). Lookaround scan: faster on 2 of 3 ((?<="|')\s+(?=[^<>\s]+=) 2.55 GiB/s vs 406.05 MiB/s, 6.42x; deleted_at 8.32 vs 6.24 GiB/s, 1.33x), slower on (?<=\d)\.(?=\S) (2.61 vs 3.12 GiB/s). Lookaround validate: password-strength 21.28 vs 65.23 ns (3.07x), username 19.94 vs 31.32 ns (1.57x). README says resharp only matches the regex crate's throughput on standard patterns.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: scripts/bench-popular-table.mts runs 'cargo run --release --features pcre2-bench --example popular-crates -- --bench'; workspace [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1. No rust-toolchain file (rust-version 1.70 minimum), so the rustc version is not stated. PCRE2 comes through the pcre2 crate 0.2.11 / pcre2-sys 0.2.10 (Cargo.lock) built with jit_if_available(true), utf(true), ucp(true); the PCRE2 library version, whether it was bundled or a system library, and its C compiler flags are not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 188 stars, 10 forks; crates.io resharp 1,891 downloads (534 recent); the .NET version resharp-dotnet is already catalogued (wave 3)
corrections.caveats: First-party table on a synthetic haystack (19 fixed lines repeated to 1 MiB), which keeps a lazy DFA's state cache warm. Rows marked with an asterisk use a rewritten pattern for resharp (the script marks rows whose resharp pattern differs): the script-tag row replaces the lazy .*? with a complement, and the lookaround rows escape underscores and dashes; resharp is leftmost-longest while PCRE2 is leftmost-first, and the benchmark never checks that the engines return the same matches. resharp returns all matches from one find_all call (allocating a Vec), while PCRE2 is driven through the Rust binding's find_iter, one FFI match call per match, which adds per-match overhead on high-match-count patterns (\d+, \w+, [A-Z]). PCRE2 wins 6 of 19 scan rows, including the script-tag row by 8.97x. PCRE2 version and C build flags are not stated. The POPL 2025 paper (ACM DOI 10.1145/3704837) evaluates the .NET implementation, not this rewrite.
corrections.why_faster: Not a language effect: resharp is a derivative-based lazy DFA (non-backtracking, leftmost-longest) against PCRE2's backtracking JIT, so the wins are on patterns where a DFA avoids backtracking or prefix rescans (e.g. \d+\.\d+\.\d+); per-match FFI calls through the Rust pcre2 binding may add to PCRE2's time on patterns with many short matches (agent reading of the benchmark source).

notes: Confirm at C; README numbers match the record except the win count (12 faster, 1 tie, 6 slower, not 13 faster) and the script-tag figure (807.97 MiB/s, not 0.81 GiB/s), both corrected; the unexplained asterisk marks rows where resharp runs a rewritten pattern. Shortcomings: synthetic repetitive haystack, different match semantics with no equality check, PCRE2 version and flags unstated, per-match FFI calls on the PCRE2 side, engine-design win not a language win. Separate Rust implementation from the catalogued resharp-dotnet with its own benchmark, so not a wrapper; the orchestrator may still treat it as a port.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine tables in the README with public benchmark code (benchmark.sh) and release-profile flags in Cargo.toml, but no CPU model, rustc version, or cut/awk implementation and version, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: benchmark.sh runs 'cargo build --release'; Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort', strip = 'debuginfo'; edition 2024, README says rustc >= 1.85.0 is required (exact rustc version not stated); default features regex and fast-lane. The system cut and awk implementations, versions and build flags are not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 821 stars, 16 forks; crates.io tuc 19,805 downloads; packaged in several distributions (repology badge)
corrections.caveats: First-party tables added to the README on 2025-09-11 (v1.3.0); the hardware, rustc version and the cut and awk implementations and versions are not stated (benchmark.sh uses GNU sed -i syntax, wget and the uutils 'coreutils' multicall binary, which suggests Linux and probably GNU cut, but this is not stated). Only the first 1,000,000 lines of HEPMASS all_train.csv are used and output goes to /dev/null, so write costs are excluded. cut cannot split on a multi-character delimiter, so that table compares against 'tr -s | cut' and awk pipelines. uutils cut (Rust) is also 3.2x faster than the system cut, and hck in literal mode is only 1.18x slower than tuc, so the gap is to the system cut's implementation rather than to C. With a regex delimiter (-e'\s+') tuc (9.870 s) is no faster than hck (9.834 s). Means of at least 5 runs after 3 warmups.
corrections.why_faster: Not a language effect: tuc's default fast-lane path (src/fast_lane.rs) finds delimiters with memchr::memchr_iter (the memchr crate's SIMD search) and stops scanning fields once the requested ones are found, and reads the input through memmap2 (the --no-mmap rows are 1.13-1.14x slower); the system cut's field loop is a plain byte-oriented stdio loop (agent knowledge, cut source not opened).

notes: Confirm at C; every quoted number matches the README tables. Shortcomings: hardware, rustc and cut versions unstated, first 1M lines only, output to /dev/null, the win is memchr SIMD scanning plus mmap rather than the language (uutils cut, also Rust, is 1.63x slower than tuc and 3.2x faster than cut). hck (sstadick/hck) and uutils/coreutils are already catalogued.
